**Lotus Sutra and the parable of the burning house**
The most-cited sutra in these questions. In its best-known parable, a rich father lures his children out of a burning house by promising them toy carts (goat, deer, and ox carts), then gives them an even better great cart; the story illustrates "skillful" or "expedient means" and the doctrine of the "One Vehicle." It also contains the parable of the herbs nourished by the same rain cloud and the phantom city conjured to motivate weary travelers.

**Upaya ("skillful means" or "expedient means")**
The Mahayana idea that the Buddha adapts his teaching to the capacities of his listeners, even using provisional truths or white lies to lead beings to enlightenment. It is the central theme of the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable.

**Diamond Sutra**
A short Perfection of Wisdom sutra whose title refers to a diamond (or "vajra") that can "cut through illusions." It opens after the Buddha returns from his daily alms round and is prompted by a question from the elder Subhuti. A printed Chinese copy from 868 CE found at Dunhuang is the oldest dated printed book.

**Heart Sutra and "form is emptiness, emptiness is form"**
A very short Perfection of Wisdom text in which the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara explains sunyata (emptiness), equating form with emptiness. It ends with the mantra "gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha," which Edward Conze translated as "Gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, O what an awakening, all hail!"

**Prajnaparamita ("Perfection of Wisdom")**
A genre of early Mahayana sutras, among the oldest Mahayana texts, that includes the Heart and Diamond Sutras. Their main teaching is sunyata, the emptiness of all phenomena.

**Subhuti**
A disciple of the Buddha whose question opens the Diamond Sutra and who serves as the Buddha's main interlocutor in many Perfection of Wisdom texts.

**"Thread" or "string"**
The literal meaning of the Sanskrit word sutra (Pali sutta), related to the root for "to sew" or "to bind." The same word is used for aphoristic texts in Hinduism, such as Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

**Second basket of the Tripitaka (Sutta Pitaka)**
The Tripitaka, or "three baskets," is the Buddhist canon. The Sutta Pitaka, the collection of the Buddha's discourses, is the second basket, between the Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules) and the Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophical analysis).

**"Thus have I heard"**
The formula that opens most sutras. It is traditionally attributed to Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, who recited the discourses from memory at the First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha shortly after the Buddha's death.

**Nichiren and Tendai schools**
Japanese Buddhist schools founded on devotion to the Lotus Sutra. Nichiren Buddhism centers on chanting the sutra's title, "Namu Myoho Renge Kyo" ("homage to the Sutra of the Lotus of the Wonderful Law"). Tendai derives from the Chinese Tiantai school, whose founder Zhiyi wrote major commentaries on the Lotus Sutra.

**Hidden among the nagas**
A traditional explanation for why Mahayana sutras appeared centuries after the Buddha: they were said to have been hidden by the nagas (serpent deities) until humanity was ready. Legend says Nagarjuna retrieved the Perfection of Wisdom sutras from the naga realm.

**Platform Sutra and the poem contest**
A Chan (Zen) text attributed to Huineng. It describes a contest in which monks wrote verses on a wall to succeed the Fifth Patriarch Hongren; the illiterate Huineng's verse won, and he became the Sixth Patriarch. Together with the Heart and Diamond Sutras, it is one of the key Zen sutras.

**Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Sermon in the Deer Park)**
The "Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma" discourse, recording the Buddha's first sermon at the Deer Park at Sarnath. In it he taught the Four Noble Truths and the Middle Way to his first five disciples.

**Xuanzang**
A 7th-century Chinese monk who traveled to India to collect Buddhist sutras and brought hundreds of texts back to China to translate. His journey inspired the novel Journey to the West.

**Kangyur**
The Tibetan Buddhist canon of texts regarded as the Buddha's words. Its Perfection of Wisdom section groups the sutras into "Six Mothers" (the longer versions) and "Eleven Children" (the shorter ones).
